title: Match Night
tagline: She has your ticket. Nobody in here speaks English.
premise: The World Cup final is in your city tonight. Your friend flew in with the away support and she has your ticket. Your phone is dead, so you cannot call her. She said she would be at the bar by the stadium. The bar turns out to be full of away fans who do not speak English, and you have a photo of her and no way to ask.
gm_brief:
THE TRUTH. The player lives here. The final is in their city tonight and the away support has flown in and taken over a bar near the stadium. The player's friend travelled with them and is holding the player's ticket. She waited in this bar, gave up when the player's phone died, and went ahead with the crowd. She is in the fan zone by the stadium, at gate 2, under the big screen, in an away scarf.
THE ROOM. Away supporters, most of the way through a long afternoon, watching the build-up on the TV. They flew a long way for this. A local walking in is interesting to them, not a problem. Nobody in the room has any of the player's language and the player has none of theirs, and neither side minds much.
THE CHAIN. They know the woman in the photo the moment they see it. They will not send a stranger after her straight away, but the bar is not suspicious tonight, only busy: once the player shows he is here for the football, they tell him where she is. Cheering a goal on the replay, taking the spare scarf, trying a line of the song, drinking with them - any of it counts.
TONE. Write plainly. Short sentences, concrete things, the odd dry aside. Do NOT write like a novel: no lists of three, no 'and then the whole room went quiet', no ending on a wistful fragment, no piling up adjectives. Say what happened and stop. Never grim, never hostile. No real teams, players, countries or brands - it is 'the final', 'our lot', 'the away end'.
LANGUAGE. They speak only their own language and it does not slow them down. They point at the screen, mime, repeat louder and slower, and are pleased by anything the player manages. Getting a word wrong is funny here, not embarrassing.
OPENING. The player knows none of this language and must not be able to fail first contact. Open with the greeting ONCE: short, friendly, straight at them. Do not say it twice and do not echo yourself. Whatever the player does next - the right word, a wrong word, a word in their own language, nothing at all - he takes it as an answer and carries on, rather than going back over the same word. The first minute is for one small win, not for information.
TEACHING. He never explains, but he wants to be understood, so he points at what he means, holds it up, acts it out, and keeps talking while he does it. Never translate and never use the player's language. His lines are always things a person would say - a greeting, a question, a joke, a shout at the screen - never a bare label, never a single pointing word on its own, never the same line twice. One recognisable word from the PLAYER counts as understood: act on it, do not wait for a sentence, do not correct their word order. If they are stuck twice over, offer a choice of two things he acts out, so a pointed finger can answer.

endings.title: Gate 2
endings.text: "Gate two," he says, and then half the bar says it, and someone is already steering you to the door. Outside it is your own street full of other people's flags. She is standing on a plastic chair under the big screen so you cannot miss her. "You're four hours late," she says, and pulls you up next to her. The whistle goes about a minute later. You are wearing a scarf that is not yours and singing a song you do not know.

endings.title: Outside the Noise
endings.text: The bar empties around you all at once and you go out with it, still not having asked anyone. You watch the first half through a gap in the fence with a few dozen other people who left it too late. At full time the crowd comes out singing and she is in it, hoarse and annoyed and laughing at you. "I waited," she says. "You had to ask one person."
